meta.name: AWS Certified Security – Specialty (SCS-C02)
meta.notes: [bulk-tag pass: added `aws-scs-c02` tag to 61 questions] [scheduled-agent hardening pass 2026-05-27: full-pack rewrite of all 61 questions — removed self-defeating distractor tails (“— does not…”), completed truncated correct options, length-balanced options within ~20%, cleaned explanation fragments, ensured each explanation states why each distractor is wrong]

questions.question: GuardDuty generates a finding 'Recon:EC2/PortProbeUnprotectedPort' for multiple EC2 instances. The security team wants to automatically isolate affected instances by removing them from their security group and placing them in a quarantine security group. What is the MOST automated implementation?
options: Create an EventBridge rule matching the GuardDuty finding type and trigger a Lambda function that swaps the instance's security groups to a quarantine SG
Set a CloudWatch alarm on GuardDuty finding metrics that triggers an SNS notification to the security team for manual remediation
Enable GuardDuty automatic-response which natively isolates EC2 instances when port-probe findings are generated
Use AWS Security Hub native automated remediation to swap instance security groups based on GuardDuty findings
questions.explanation: GuardDuty does not natively isolate instances and Security Hub does not perform that remediation either; the standard pattern is an EventBridge rule that matches the specific finding type and triggers a Lambda function which uses the EC2 API to detach the production security group and attach a quarantine SG. A manual SNS notification is slower and not automated. Neither GuardDuty nor Security Hub ships a built-in 'isolate EC2' action — both raise findings that you wire to your own remediation.

questions.question: A security engineer needs to investigate a potential security incident involving unauthorized S3 API calls. The engineer needs to determine which IAM entity made specific calls, from which IP addresses, and at what times — going back 90 days. Which service provides this data most efficiently?
options: Amazon Detective, which ingests CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs and GuardDuty findings to build entity behaviour graphs and visualize activity timelines for an IAM principal
AWS Config resource history, which records S3 bucket configuration changes (encryption, policy, ACL) over time for audit
CloudTrail Event History in the AWS console, which is searchable but limited to the 90-day default lookback
CloudTrail Lake with SQL queries against an event data store containing management and data events for the 90-day window
questions.explanation: Amazon Detective automatically ingests CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs and GuardDuty findings and correlates them into behaviour graphs, surfacing per-principal API timelines, source IPs and resource access without manual querying — purpose-built for investigations. AWS Config tracks resource configuration changes, not who called which API. CloudTrail Event History gives raw events but no correlation and only 90-day search. CloudTrail Lake supports rich SQL but you must write the queries yourself; Detective is more efficient for this investigative workflow.

questions.question: A company is experiencing a suspected DDoS attack targeting its web application on EC2 behind an ALB. The attack is a volumetric UDP flood at layer 3. AWS Shield Standard is already enabled. What additional measure provides DDoS-specific financial protection and 24/7 access to the AWS DDoS Response Team (DRT)?
options: Place CloudFront in front of the ALB to absorb the volumetric attack at the edge using AWS's global capacity
Upgrade to AWS Shield Advanced on the ALB to gain DDoS cost protection credits and 24/7 DRT engagement
Configure AWS Network Firewall with Suricata rules that drop UDP flood traffic before it reaches the ALB
Enable AWS WAF with rate-based rules on the ALB to limit high-volume UDP traffic to the application
questions.explanation: Only AWS Shield Advanced provides DDoS cost protection (service credits for scaling charges incurred during an attack) and 24/7 access to the DDoS Response Team — both are paid-tier features tied to Shield Advanced subscriptions. CloudFront absorbs volumetric traffic but doesn't add DRT access or cost credits on its own. Network Firewall and WAF rate-based rules help mitigate specific traffic patterns but neither gives you the DRT or financial protection.

questions.question: A security team receives a GuardDuty finding 'UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/ConsoleLoginSuccess.B' indicating a console login from an unusual location. The security engineer needs to determine what actions the user took after logging in. Which sequence of tools investigates this most effectively?
options: Use AWS Config change history filtered to resources modified by the IAM user during the suspicious window
Query CloudTrail event history for all API calls by the IAM principal after the login, then pivot into Amazon Detective for a correlated behaviour graph
Review the IAM user's access-key last-used data in the IAM console and search the CloudWatch agent logs from EC2
Query GuardDuty findings only, filtering to that user account ID and the period after the suspicious login
questions.explanation: The recommended flow is to use the GuardDuty finding to identify the principal and source IP, query CloudTrail for the principal's subsequent API calls, then open Amazon Detective to visualise the principal's behaviour graph against historical baseline. AWS Config records configuration changes but misses non-config API actions. Access-key last-used data is single-point metadata, not a per-call audit trail. GuardDuty alone only shows findings it has produced — most post-login activity won't appear there at all.

questions.question: A company wants to continuously monitor for publicly exposed S3 buckets, open security groups (port 22/3389 to 0.0.0.0/0), and unencrypted RDS databases across all accounts in their AWS Organization. Which service provides this continuous compliance monitoring with the least custom code?
options: AWS Config managed rules (s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited, restricted-ssh, rds-storage-encrypted) deployed via StackSets and aggregated in Security Hub
Lambda functions triggered by EventBridge on a schedule to inspect each resource type and write JSON findings to a central S3 bucket per account
AWS Inspector continuously scanning all EC2 instances, RDS databases and other supported workloads for these security and compliance misconfigurations
AWS Trusted Advisor security category checks pulled from each member account on a periodic schedule into a single central organisation dashboard
questions.explanation: AWS Config managed rules are evaluation-as-code maintained by AWS for these exact checks; deploying them with CloudFormation StackSets to every account and aggregating with Security Hub gives organisation-wide continuous compliance with zero custom code. Schedule-driven Lambda is custom code you must maintain. Inspector targets software vulnerabilities (CVEs) on EC2/ECR, not S3 public-access or RDS encryption configuration. Trusted Advisor offers a fixed set of high-level checks and doesn't cover all three resource types at the granularity required.

questions.question: A CloudTrail data event is required to log all S3 GetObject API calls on a specific bucket containing PII data. The security team also wants to detect when someone downloads more than 1,000 objects in a 5-minute window. Which combination achieves both requirements?
options: Configure Amazon Macie to monitor GetObject API calls and alert on high-volume download patterns from a single principal
Enable S3 Event Notifications for GetObject events into SNS, then use CloudWatch Metric Math to count the messages
Enable S3 server access logging to a target bucket and have a Lambda function parse the log files to count GetObject calls
Enable CloudTrail data events for the S3 bucket sending to CloudWatch Logs, create a metric filter on GetObject and alarm when the count exceeds 1,000 in 5 minutes
questions.explanation: S3 object-level operations (GetObject/PutObject) are CloudTrail data events, off by default; enabling them for the bucket, streaming to CloudWatch Logs and adding a metric filter + alarm gives you a managed, near-real-time counter for the threshold. Macie detects sensitive data and unusual S3 access patterns but isn't a configurable per-bucket GetObject counter. S3 Event Notifications fire on object events but not on GetObject and can't be sized into 5-minute windows trivially. S3 server access logs have delivery delay and gaps and aren't suitable for real-time threshold alarms.

questions.question: A security engineer needs to query 18 months of CloudTrail history using SQL to find all IAM role creations across 50 AWS accounts. CloudTrail Lake has been configured. Which approach is correct?
options: Use Amazon Detective to search IAM role creation events across all linked accounts over the 18-month period
Query the aggregated CloudTrail log files in S3 using Amazon Athena with a Glue table over the trail prefix
Use CloudTrail Event History in the console, which supports an 18-month lookback by default for organisation trails
Run a SQL query against the CloudTrail Lake organisation event data store filtering eventName = 'CreateRole' and a time range of 18 months
questions.explanation: CloudTrail Lake is the managed, SQL-queryable, immutable event data store; an organisation event data store ingests events from every member account and supports retention up to 7 years, so a single SQL query against it solves the problem. Detective is investigation-oriented and not built for ad-hoc SQL audit queries. Athena over the raw S3 log files works but requires Glue/table maintenance and isn't the 'CloudTrail Lake is configured' answer. CloudTrail Event History is limited to 90 days, not 18 months.

questions.question: A security engineer wants to detect when any VPC security group is modified to allow inbound traffic from 0.0.0.0/0 on port 3389 (RDP). The detection must occur within 2 minutes of the change. Which solution provides this near-real-time detection?
options: Run an AWS Config rule on a 5-minute schedule that evaluates every security group for open RDP ingress
Enable Amazon GuardDuty, which automatically generates a finding whenever a security group is changed to expose RDP
Create an EventBridge rule on the CloudTrail 'AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress' event with a pattern matching port 3389 from 0.0.0.0/0, target a Lambda or SNS
Use the AWS Config managed rule 'restricted-common-ports' wired to SNS notifications for failed evaluations
questions.explanation: EventBridge delivers CloudTrail management events in roughly 15–30 seconds, so an event-pattern rule that matches AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress with port 3389 and 0.0.0.0/0 gives well-under-two-minute detection. A 5-minute Config schedule fails the latency requirement. GuardDuty focuses on threat intel and behavioural findings, not configuration change detection on security groups. The 'restricted-common-ports' Config rule evaluates periodically (minutes) and isn't near-real-time.

questions.question: AWS Config detects that an EC2 instance is using an unapproved AMI. The security team wants the non-compliant instance to be automatically stopped within 10 minutes of detection. Which configuration implements this auto-remediation?
options: Use AWS Systems Manager Compliance to automatically stop EC2 instances whose AMI ID is not on the approved list
Attach the SSM Automation document 'AWS-StopEC2Instance' as the auto-remediation action on the AWS Config rule that evaluates approved AMIs
Create an EventBridge rule on AWS Config non-compliance events that sends an SNS notification to the operations team for manual action
Create a Lambda function that polls AWS Config every 10 minutes for non-compliant resources and stops each one found
questions.explanation: AWS Config supports native auto-remediation by associating an SSM Automation document with a rule; the managed 'AWS-StopEC2Instance' document stops the instance when the rule reports NON_COMPLIANT, satisfying the time requirement without custom code. Systems Manager Compliance reports patch/state compliance but doesn't enforce approved-AMI policies by stopping instances. SNS-only notification is manual, not auto-remediation. A scheduled Lambda is feasible but is the highest-overhead option and isn't the AWS Config–native approach.

questions.question: A security engineer needs to prove to auditors that their AWS environment meets the CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark. The evidence must include per-control compliance status for all 50 accounts in the organization. Which service generates this compliance evidence most efficiently?
options: Enable AWS Security Hub with the 'CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark' standard across all accounts using Organizations integration to get per-control pass/fail status
Use AWS Audit Manager with its pre-built CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark framework to automatically collect per-control evidence packaged as an audit-ready report
Deploy AWS Config conformance packs matching CIS controls via StackSets to every account and export the compliance summary
Run AWS Trusted Advisor security checks in each account and manually export the results into a single spreadsheet
questions.explanation: Audit Manager is purpose-built for compliance evidence collection: its pre-built CIS AWS Foundations framework maps controls to AWS API/Config/Security Hub/CloudTrail signals and produces an audit-ready assessment report per control, per account — exactly the evidence auditors expect. Security Hub shows live compliance scores but isn't an evidence-packaging tool. Config conformance packs evaluate controls but don't generate framework-mapped audit evidence. Trusted Advisor checks are a small, fixed list and don't cover the full CIS benchmark.

questions.question: A company wants to restrict all AWS API calls to originate only from the company's corporate IP range (203.0.113.0/24). All other API calls from any source should be denied. Where should this restriction be applied for the STRONGEST enforcement?
options: Add an IAM permission boundary to all IAM users requiring an aws:SourceIp condition on every API call
Enable AWS CloudTrail and have EventBridge real-time rules detect API calls from unknown IPs and trigger Lambda revocation
Configure an identity-based IAM policy on each IAM user and role that denies access when aws:SourceIp is outside the corporate range
Create a Service Control Policy at the organization root with Deny on all actions when aws:SourceIp is not in 203.0.113.0/24 (with an aws:ViaAWSService exception)
questions.explanation: An SCP at the organisation root is the strongest control because it applies to every principal in every member account — including account-level admins and root users — and cannot be overridden by lower-level IAM policies. Permission boundaries only constrain individual IAM entities and don't apply to root users. EventBridge-on-CloudTrail is detective and reactive, not preventive. Per-identity policies must be replicated to every principal and can be undone by any account admin.

questions.question: An application's Lambda function needs to call an external SaaS API that requires basic authentication. The API credentials should be securely stored, automatically rotated every 30 days, and NOT appear in environment variables or code. Which service provides this with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: KMS-encrypt the credentials and bake the ciphertext into the Lambda deployment package, decrypting at runtime
Store the credentials in an S3 object encrypted with KMS and have Lambda fetch and decrypt them on every invocation
Store the credentials in AWS Secrets Manager with a rotation Lambda configured for a 30-day schedule, calling GetSecretValue at runtime
Store the credentials in SSM Parameter Store SecureString and retrieve them via the SSM GetParameter API at runtime
questions.explanation: Secrets Manager natively supports scheduled rotation via a Lambda rotation function — for a SaaS credential you write a small rotator that creates the new credential at the SaaS side and updates the secret on the configured cadence; the function calls GetSecretValue without env vars. Baking ciphertext into the deployment package or fetching from S3 each call works but adds custom code and isn't natively rotatable. SSM Parameter Store SecureString lacks native automatic rotation — you'd have to build it yourself.

questions.question: A security engineer is evaluating IAM policy logic. A user has an identity-based policy that allows s3:GetObject on a specific bucket. A resource-based policy on the same bucket explicitly Denies s3:GetObject for that user. What is the effective permission?
options: Allow — resource-based policies only restrict cross-account access, so they don't affect same-account principals
Deny — an explicit Deny in ANY policy (identity, resource, SCP, boundary, session) always overrides any Allow
It depends on the order in which the policies were attached and the most recent one wins
Allow — the identity-based Allow always takes precedence over a resource-based Deny in the same account
questions.explanation: AWS IAM evaluation logic is unambiguous: an explicit Deny in any policy type wins over any Allow, and the default is implicit Deny. Resource-based policies apply within the same account too. There is no attachment-order rule — Deny vs Allow is independent of order. There is no general precedence of identity policies over resource policies — both are combined, and an explicit Deny in either ends the request.

questions.question: A company needs to grant a third-party auditing firm temporary read-only access to their AWS account for a 2-week audit. The auditors have their own AWS account. What is the MOST secure approach?
options: Create temporary IAM users for each auditor with ReadOnlyAccess and share the long-term credentials via encrypted email
Share the company's AWS root account credentials with the lead auditor for the duration of the engagement
Create an IAM role in the company's account with ReadOnlyAccess and a trust policy allowing the auditors' AWS account to call sts:AssumeRole
Create an IAM user with programmatic access only and share the access key and secret key directly with the firm
questions.explanation: Cross-account IAM role assumption is the AWS-recommended pattern for third-party access: the auditors call sts:AssumeRole from their own account to receive short-lived credentials, the role can be deleted at audit end, and every call is logged in CloudTrail under an AssumedRole identity. IAM users with shared long-term credentials have no expiry guarantees and can leak. Sharing root credentials is never appropriate. Sharing access keys for a single IAM user gives the firm long-term credentials with no per-user attribution.

questions.question: A security engineer needs to create an IAM policy that allows EC2 instance start/stop only when the instance has a specific tag (Environment = Production) AND the request comes from the us-east-1 region. Which IAM policy condition block achieves this?
options: Create two separate IAM policies — one for the region condition, one for the tag condition — and attach both to the IAM identity
Use a single Condition with ArnLike on the resource ARN, encoding both region and tag into the ARN pattern
Use a single Condition block with StringEquals on aws:RequestedRegion AND ec2:ResourceTag/Environment, so both keys must match
Use a Condition with StringEquals on aws:SourceIp for the region and aws:ResourceTag for the tag
questions.explanation: Multiple condition keys inside the same Condition operator block are evaluated with logical AND, so combining aws:RequestedRegion = us-east-1 with ec2:ResourceTag/Environment = Production exactly expresses 'both must hold'. Splitting into two policies still ANDs at the policy level but is harder to manage and isn't the canonical form. Encoding tags or regions into an ARN pattern doesn't work because tags and regions aren't part of the ARN structure that way. aws:SourceIp is the caller's IP, not the AWS region of the call.

questions.question: An organization uses AWS IAM Identity Center (SSO) with their Active Directory as the identity source. A developer needs temporary credentials to access AWS via CLI. What is the recommended method?
options: Have the developer call sts:AssumeRole with their IAM username and password from the CLI
Run 'aws configure sso' once and then 'aws sso login', which retrieves IAM Identity Center temporary credentials via a browser flow
Create a permanent IAM user for the developer and share long-term access keys for the CLI profile
Generate an IAM Identity Center SAML assertion manually and extract the temporary credentials from its response
questions.explanation: AWS CLI v2 has native IAM Identity Center support: 'aws configure sso' wires up the profile and 'aws sso login' opens a browser, authenticates against AD via Identity Center and caches refreshable short-lived credentials. sts:AssumeRole doesn't accept usernames and passwords — it requires existing credentials and an STS API call. Long-term IAM user access keys defeat the purpose of SSO. Manually extracting SAML assertions is unsupported and brittle when the CLI has a built-in flow.

questions.question: A company's S3 bucket stores confidential financial records. The security team requires that objects can NEVER be deleted or overwritten for 7 years, even by the bucket owner or AWS root account. Which S3 feature enforces this?
options: S3 Versioning with MFA Delete enabled so permanent deletes require an MFA-authenticated root call
An S3 Bucket Policy with explicit Deny on s3:DeleteObject and s3:PutObject for all principals including the root account
S3 Object Lock in Governance mode with a 7-year retention period and tightly restricted bypass permissions
S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode with a 7-year retention period so no user — including root — can delete or overwrite before expiry
questions.explanation: S3 Object Lock Compliance mode is true WORM: once set, retention cannot be shortened or bypassed by any user including the AWS root, satisfying SEC 17a-4 / FINRA-style requirements. MFA Delete adds friction but the root user can still authorise deletion with MFA. A bucket policy Deny can be edited by anyone with PutBucketPolicy (including root) and so isn't truly immutable. Governance mode allows holders of s3:BypassGovernanceRetention to delete, which violates the 'even by root' requirement.

questions.question: A security engineer needs to ensure all data stored in an S3 bucket is encrypted with a specific CMK, and any PutObject request without SSE-KMS using that key is rejected. How should the bucket policy be written?
options: Enable default bucket encryption with SSE-KMS and the CMK and rely on it to reject any non-KMS uploads automatically
Write a KMS key policy that allows the Encrypt action only when the request originates from that specific S3 bucket
Write a bucket policy that allows all s3:PutObject calls and let KMS enforce that the data was encrypted properly
Write a bucket policy that Denies s3:PutObject when s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption is not 'aws:kms' OR the kms-key-id header is not the specific CMK ARN
questions.explanation: Default encryption applies SSE-KMS if no header is provided but does not reject a PutObject that explicitly specifies a different algorithm or key, so an explicit-Deny bucket policy on the two relevant request headers is required for strict enforcement. KMS key policies authorise key use but don't reject S3 uploads that bypass KMS. Allowing all PutObject and 'trusting KMS' doesn't enforce the algorithm header at all. The bucket policy is the right control because that's where the request headers can be evaluated.

questions.question: A company needs to manage TLS certificates for 200 internal microservices using custom domain names within their VPC. Certificates should auto-renew and be provisioned by application developers without requiring IAM privilege escalation. Which service provides this?
options: CloudHSM hosting a custom PKI implementation for internal certificate issuance and lifecycle management
The legacy IAM certificate store used for uploading SSL/TLS certificates accessible to application teams
ACM public certificates issued via DNS validation, used for all internal-only service domains
AWS Private CA (ACM Private CA) for the private CA hierarchy with ACM issuing and auto-renewing private certificates for internal services
questions.explanation: AWS Private CA (formerly ACM Private CA) is the managed private CA service; ACM issues, renews and distributes private certificates for internal domains, and developers can request them without holding the CA private key. CloudHSM can host custom PKI but you operate it yourself with no managed renewal. The IAM certificate store is legacy and supports only uploads, no issuance or renewal. ACM public certificates require public DNS validation and aren't usable for internal-only names.

questions.question: A KMS customer-managed key (CMK) is used to encrypt S3 data. A security engineer needs to allow Application Team A to encrypt data but prevent them from ever decrypting it. Which IAM/KMS permission combination achieves this?
options: Grant only kms:GenerateDataKey on the CMK, on the assumption that S3 will encrypt on the team's behalf without granting decrypt rights
Grant only kms:Encrypt on the CMK, with no kms:Decrypt and no kms:GenerateDataKey, and rely on S3 to perform envelope encryption directly
In the key policy, allow kms:Encrypt and kms:GenerateDataKey for the team and explicitly Deny kms:Decrypt and kms:GenerateDataKeyWithoutPlaintext
Grant the team both kms:Encrypt and kms:Decrypt but restrict kms:Decrypt with an aws:SourceIp condition matching unused IP ranges
questions.explanation: S3 envelope encryption needs kms:GenerateDataKey, not just kms:Encrypt; granting Encrypt + GenerateDataKey and explicitly denying Decrypt (and the plaintext-less variant for completeness) yields true 'write-only' use of the key, because an explicit Deny in the key policy cannot be overridden. Granting only GenerateDataKey misses the key-policy Deny that prevents future grants of Decrypt elsewhere. Granting only Encrypt breaks S3's envelope flow. Restricting Decrypt by 'unused IP' is fragile and not a real Deny.

questions.question: A company requires that an RDS MySQL database connection uses TLS and that the certificate is validated by the application. The certificate is from the AWS RDS CA. How should the application enforce this?
options: Set 'require_secure_transport = ON' in the RDS parameter group and configure the MySQL client with ssl-ca pointing to the downloaded AWS RDS CA bundle
Configure the security group to only allow inbound port 3306 from the application subnet, on the assumption that closed SG = enforced TLS
Enable RDS encryption at rest on the instance, which also enables in-transit encryption for client connections automatically
Enable Multi-AZ for the RDS instance because Multi-AZ deployments automatically enforce TLS for all client connections
questions.explanation: Two independent enforcement points are needed: the database parameter 'require_secure_transport = ON' rejects non-TLS connections at the server, and the MySQL client must validate the server certificate against the AWS RDS root CA bundle (ssl-ca) so a MITM can't substitute its own cert. A security group only restricts the source of the TCP connection, not whether it's TLS. RDS encryption at rest and TLS in transit are configured independently. Multi-AZ is for availability and has nothing to do with TLS.

questions.question: A company needs to scan all Docker images pushed to Amazon ECR for known CVEs before they are deployed to ECS. Vulnerable images (CRITICAL/HIGH CVEs) should be blocked from deployment. Which architecture achieves this?
options: Enable Amazon Inspector v2 ECR scanning on push, then have an EventBridge rule trigger a Lambda on CRITICAL/HIGH findings to update the ECR image tag or block deployment
Configure AWS CodeBuild in the CI/CD pipeline to run 'docker scan' before pushing, and rely on its exit code to fail the build for any CVE found
Use AWS Security Hub to scan ECR images and block deployments by validating the ECS task definition at deploy time
Enable ECR basic scanning, which automatically quarantines and refuses to serve images that have critical CVEs after push
questions.explanation: Amazon Inspector v2 is the managed container vulnerability scanner: it scans ECR images on push, continuously rescans as new CVEs are published, and emits findings to EventBridge — a Lambda on CRITICAL/HIGH findings can gate deployment (e.g. by mutating image tags or updating a deploy-allow list). docker scan inside CodeBuild misses CVEs published after the build runs. Security Hub aggregates findings but doesn't scan images. ECR basic scanning surfaces findings but does not quarantine or block pulls.

questions.question: A security architect needs to deploy an inline network security inspection layer for all traffic entering and leaving a VPC. The solution must be transparent to applications and support third-party IDS/IPS appliances. Which AWS service provides this architecture?
options: Deploy AWS Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB) with third-party virtual appliances behind it, using GWLB endpoints in route tables to send traffic inline through the appliances
Configure VPC Traffic Mirroring to copy all traffic to a third-party IDS appliance running in a separate VPC for analysis
Place AWS WAF on the Application Load Balancer to inspect inbound HTTP and HTTPS traffic for the protected applications
Deploy AWS Network Firewall in the VPC and direct all traffic through it via route table modifications for inbound and outbound flows
questions.explanation: Gateway Load Balancer is purpose-built to scale third-party virtual appliances (firewalls, IDS/IPS, DPI) inline using the GENEVE protocol; route tables steer traffic through GWLB endpoints transparently. Traffic Mirroring is passive — it copies traffic and cannot drop or modify it. WAF is HTTP/HTTPS-only and bound to ALB/CloudFront/API Gateway, not a generic inline network inspection layer. AWS Network Firewall is an AWS-managed appliance, not 'third-party IDS/IPS support'.

questions.question: An EC2 instance in a private subnet needs to access the S3 service API without traffic traversing the internet or requiring a NAT Gateway. The solution must not allow the instance to reach non-S3 AWS services. Which architecture satisfies these requirements?
options: Create an S3 gateway VPC endpoint in the VPC, with an endpoint policy that scopes access to specific S3 actions/buckets and routes only S3 prefixes via the endpoint
Create an S3 interface VPC endpoint (PrivateLink) so all S3 API calls leave the VPC through an ENI that bridges to other AWS services too
Deploy a NAT Gateway in a public subnet and restrict the private route table to allow only the published S3 IP ranges
Configure a Site-to-Site VPN connection to AWS and route S3 traffic over the VPN tunnel rather than the internet
questions.explanation: An S3 gateway VPC endpoint adds an S3-only prefix list to the route table, so only S3 traffic leaves via the endpoint and other AWS services aren't reachable through it; an endpoint policy further restricts which actions and buckets the endpoint allows. An S3 interface endpoint solves the same connectivity problem but costs more and doesn't generalise to other services on its own. NAT Gateway works but does not satisfy 'no traffic traversing the internet' and doesn't naturally restrict to S3. A VPN reaches your on-prem network, not the S3 service.

questions.question: A company has deployed an Application Load Balancer accessible from the internet. The security team wants to block traffic from countries known for malicious activity while allowing a specific IP range from a partner to bypass the geographic restriction. Which AWS WAF configuration achieves this?
options: Create two separate WAF web ACLs — one for the geographic block and one for the partner IP allow — and attach both to the ALB
Configure a NACL to block traffic from country IP ranges, because AWS WAF does not support geographic match rules natively
Use AWS Shield Advanced geographic filtering combined with a WAF IP-set allowlist to override the geo filter for the partner range
Create one WAF web ACL with Rule 1 (priority 1) Allow on the partner IP set and Rule 2 (priority 2) Block on a GeoMatch rule for blocked countries, then attach it to the ALB
questions.explanation: WAF evaluates rules in priority order and stops at the first terminating action; placing Allow on the partner IP set at priority 1 lets partner traffic through before the geo block at priority 2 rejects everything else from the listed countries. A WAF only allows one web ACL per resource, so two ACLs on one ALB isn't a valid option. NACLs operate by IP address ranges, not by country code. Shield Advanced doesn't have its own geo-filter that bypasses WAF.

questions.question: A company's AWS Firewall Manager administrator needs to enforce WAF rules across all 30 accounts in their organization. New accounts that join should automatically have the WAF rules applied. Which service and configuration enables this?
options: Manually create matching WAF web ACLs in each account and use an AWS Config rule to flag accounts that don't have them
Configure AWS Firewall Manager with a WAF policy scoped to the organization or selected OUs so new accounts inherit the policy automatically
Use AWS Control Tower guardrails to enforce a baseline WAF web ACL deployment across all accounts in the landing zone
Use CloudFormation StackSets to deploy WAF web ACLs to every account, with automatic deployment enabled to target newly joined accounts
questions.explanation: Firewall Manager is the AWS-native service for centrally managing WAF, Shield Advanced, security groups, Network Firewall and Route 53 Resolver policies across an Organization; policies target OUs and automatically apply to new accounts that join. Manual ACL creation per account doesn't auto-apply to new accounts. Control Tower guardrails don't cover WAF web ACL distribution. StackSets with auto-deployment can ship resources but lacks Firewall Manager's policy compliance evaluation and remediation specifically for WAF.

questions.question: A security engineer finds that an EC2 instance in a public subnet is sending large volumes of outbound traffic to an external IP. GuardDuty has a finding 'Behavior:EC2/NetworkPortUnusual'. What should be the FIRST remediation action?
options: Terminate the EC2 instance immediately to stop the outbound traffic and prevent further damage
Strip all permissions from the instance's IAM role so any AWS-API-based exfiltration paths stop working
Reboot the instance so any malware processes resident in memory are terminated before investigation
Isolate the instance by attaching a quarantine security group that denies all traffic and snapshot the EBS volume before further action
questions.explanation: Incident response best practice is contain then investigate: a quarantine security group blocking all traffic stops further damage while keeping the instance alive so an EBS snapshot preserves volatile and on-disk forensic evidence. Terminating destroys evidence. Stripping the IAM role addresses only AWS-API-based exfiltration, not the active network outbound flow. Rebooting can clear memory artifacts that an investigator would want to capture.

questions.question: A security engineer needs to configure a Network ACL to allow inbound HTTP (port 80) requests to a web server in the subnet. The NACL must also allow the return traffic. Which NACL rules are required?
options: One inbound rule allowing TCP port 80 from 0.0.0.0/0, with the assumption that NACLs are stateful and return traffic is handled automatically
Inbound rule allowing TCP port 80 from 0.0.0.0/0 and an outbound rule allowing TCP ephemeral ports (1024-65535) to 0.0.0.0/0 for the responses
Inbound rule allowing all TCP traffic and an outbound rule allowing all TCP traffic, because NACLs cannot be scoped granularly per port
Inbound rule allowing TCP port 80 from 0.0.0.0/0 and an outbound rule allowing TCP port 80 to 0.0.0.0/0 for the responses
questions.explanation: NACLs are stateless, so the response flow has to be explicitly permitted; clients use ephemeral source ports (1024-65535) for their HTTP requests, so the web server's TCP responses are destined for those ports and the outbound rule must allow them. The 'NACLs are stateful' claim is wrong — that's security groups. Allowing all TCP both ways is permissive and not minimum-required. Allowing outbound TCP 80 is wrong because the response destination port is the client's ephemeral port, not 80.

questions.question: A company runs a multi-tier web application. The database tier contains credit card data. Per PCI DSS requirements, the cardholder data environment (CDE) must be segmented from other systems. Which AWS architecture BEST enforces this segmentation?
options: Encrypt the RDS instance at rest with a CMK on the assumption that PCI DSS treats encrypted data stores as out of scope for segmentation
Place the database tier in a dedicated VPC with no peering to other VPCs and reach it only via tightly scoped PrivateLink or Transit Gateway routes
Deploy the database in a private subnet of the application VPC with a NACL that allows inbound only from the web-tier subnet CIDR
Use a dedicated security group on the database tier with inbound rules referencing only the web-tier security group as the source
questions.explanation: PCI DSS demands real network segmentation of the CDE from non-CDE systems; a dedicated VPC with no peering plus controlled PrivateLink/Transit Gateway routes is the strongest enforcement. Encryption at rest does not remove a system from PCI scope. Subnet + NACL gives logical separation but inside the same VPC, so it's weaker than a separate VPC and is not generally considered adequate CDE segmentation on its own. Security-group-based isolation is a tier control but doesn't constitute network segmentation under PCI.

questions.question: An application uses AWS STS to vend temporary credentials. The credentials have a default expiry of 1 hour. A security engineer wants to revoke active sessions for a specific IAM role if its credentials are suspected to be compromised. Which approach immediately revokes all active sessions for that role?
options: Call a dedicated sts:RevokeTemporaryCredentials API to invalidate every outstanding token issued for the role
Attach an inline policy to the role with Deny on '*' conditioned on aws:TokenIssueTime being earlier than the current timestamp
Rotate the IAM role's underlying secret key so that all previously issued credentials are invalidated
Delete the IAM role and recreate it with the same name so every active assumed-role session is terminated
questions.explanation: STS tokens cannot be revoked directly because they are stateless signed credentials; AWS's published 'revoke active sessions' pattern attaches a policy to the role that denies everything for tokens whose aws:TokenIssueTime is earlier than 'now', invalidating every previously issued session without affecting fresh ones. There is no sts:RevokeTemporaryCredentials API. IAM roles don't have a 'secret key' to rotate. Deleting and recreating the role drops existing trust policies and disrupts services unnecessarily.

questions.question: A company uses AWS Organizations with 20 accounts. Each account must have CloudTrail enabled with logs sent to a central S3 bucket in the security account. Account administrators should NOT be able to disable CloudTrail or modify the trail. Which configuration achieves this?
options: Deploy an EventBridge rule per account that detects CloudTrail StopLogging events and automatically re-enables the trail via a Lambda
Create an organization trail from the management account so it applies to all current and future member accounts and cannot be disabled by them
Use CloudFormation StackSets to deploy per-account trails and add an SCP that denies cloudtrail:StopLogging and cloudtrail:DeleteTrail
Enable the AWS Config managed rule 'cloud-trail-enabled' in every account with auto-remediation that recreates the trail if it gets disabled
questions.explanation: An organisation trail created from the management account propagates to every member account, AWS prevents member admins from disabling, modifying or deleting it, and all events are centralised in one S3 bucket — the simplest authoritative control. EventBridge-and-Lambda is reactive (a window of disabled logging always exists). StackSets + SCP works but is more moving parts than the single organisation-trail mechanism. A Config managed rule with auto-remediation is also reactive and per-account.

questions.question: A company's security team receives a notification from AWS Abuse that an EC2 instance is being used for cryptocurrency mining. The notification includes the instance ID. Using the AWS incident response playbook, what should the security engineer do FIRST?
options: Notify the instance owner and wait for them to investigate and remediate the workload themselves
Verify the instance ID belongs to the account, then contain it: detach from Auto Scaling, attach a quarantine security group and snapshot the EBS volume
Increase the CloudWatch billing alarm threshold to absorb the unexpected compute cost while the investigation proceeds
Immediately terminate the EC2 instance so the cryptocurrency mining stops as soon as possible
questions.explanation: AWS's incident response process is Contain → Eradicate → Recover → Learn; first verify the resource belongs to the account, then contain — detach from ASG so it isn't replaced, swap to a quarantine SG, and snapshot the volume to preserve forensic evidence. Owner notification alone is too slow. Adjusting a billing alarm is administrative, not a containment action. Immediate termination loses the forensic evidence needed to understand how the instance was compromised.

questions.question: Amazon Macie is enabled on an S3 bucket containing employee records. Macie generates a finding that a file contains Social Security Numbers (SSNs). The security team wants to be automatically notified and have the object's ACL set to private if it was accidentally made public. Which integration achieves this?
options: Configure Macie to natively remediate findings by setting the object ACL to private and sending an SNS notification at the same time
Route Macie findings to AWS Security Hub, which automatically remediates S3 public-access issues via its native action
Enable S3 Block Public Access at the account level so the object cannot be public regardless of its ACL setting
Create an EventBridge rule on Macie SensitiveData:S3Object/Personal findings that triggers a Lambda to inspect and reset the object ACL, then publishes an SNS notification
questions.explanation: Macie emits all findings to EventBridge; an EventBridge rule filtered on the SensitiveData:S3Object/Personal finding type can trigger a Lambda that inspects the object's ACL and resets it with PutObjectAcl, plus publish an SNS notification — Macie itself does not remediate. Security Hub aggregates findings but doesn't auto-remediate S3 ACLs. Account-level Block Public Access is a preventive control but doesn't react specifically to a Macie finding and doesn't notify the team.

questions.question: A company's developer accidentally committed AWS access keys to a public GitHub repository 2 hours ago. What are the FIRST two immediate actions the security engineer should take?
options: Deactivate (and then delete) the exposed IAM access key, and review CloudTrail filtered to that access key ID for any unauthorised activity in the exposure window
Enable GuardDuty in the account so any future unauthorised use of the exposed credentials is detected
File a GitHub DMCA takedown request to remove the credentials from the repository history before doing anything else
Rotate the access key in IAM (create new, mark old inactive) but leave the old key alive briefly until the application has switched over
questions.explanation: Immediate deactivation stops ongoing use within seconds, followed by deletion to remove the key permanently; CloudTrail's AccessKeyID filter lets you scope investigation to exactly what that key did during the exposure window. GuardDuty might detect later abuse but doesn't stop the leak. A DMCA takedown is slow and doesn't matter once the key is deactivated. Leaving the old key alive 'briefly' is exactly the window an attacker exploits — deactivate first, fix the application after.

questions.question: A company must ensure that all EBS volumes attached to EC2 instances are encrypted. New volumes should be encrypted by default and existing unencrypted volumes must be identified. Which combination of controls achieves both requirements?
options: Use EC2 launch templates that require EBS encryption so new instances cannot launch with unencrypted volumes from any account
Apply an SCP across the organization that denies ec2:CreateVolume whenever the ec2:Encrypted request key is false for new volume requests
Enable 'EBS encryption by default' at the account level per region and use the AWS Config rule 'encrypted-volumes' to report existing non-compliant volumes
Write KMS key policies that deny use of the key for any EBS volume creation request that does not include the SSE-KMS encryption header
questions.explanation: 'EBS encryption by default' is the per-region account setting that automatically encrypts all new volumes/snapshots/copies, and the AWS Config managed rule 'encrypted-volumes' evaluates every attached volume for compliance, surfacing existing unencrypted ones — together they cover both new and existing. Launch templates can require encryption but only for launches that use them. An SCP works but blocks creation rather than surfacing existing volumes. KMS key policies authorise key use; they don't enforce that EBS chose to use a key in the first place.

questions.question: A company uses CloudHSM for storing cryptographic keys. What is the PRIMARY difference between CloudHSM and AWS KMS when selecting between them?
options: KMS is multi-tenant (FIPS 140-2 Level 2) with native AWS service integration; CloudHSM is single-tenant Level 3 HSMs in your VPC where AWS has no key access
CloudHSM is cheaper than KMS for typical high-volume application encryption operations on data and integrates with all AWS services natively
KMS uses FIPS 140-2 Level 3 validated hardware whereas CloudHSM relies on purely software-based key storage backed by an HSM emulator inside your VPC
CloudHSM is a fully AWS-managed black box service while KMS requires the customer to manage and patch their own underlying key infrastructure
questions.explanation: The fundamental distinction is tenancy and FIPS level: KMS is multi-tenant Level 2 with deep native AWS service integration, while CloudHSM is single-tenant Level 3 dedicated hardware in your VPC where AWS has no key access — pick CloudHSM when regulators demand Level 3 or exclusive key control. CloudHSM is generally more expensive per operation, not cheaper. KMS isn't Level 3 and CloudHSM isn't 'software-based'. CloudHSM is partially managed by you (cluster admins, users); KMS is the fully AWS-managed service.

questions.question: A company wants to centrally manage access to all AWS accounts for 500 employees using their existing Microsoft Active Directory. Employees should be able to access multiple accounts with a single sign-on. Which AWS service provides this with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Use AWS Directory Service Simple AD to replicate the on-prem AD into AWS and share it directly with each member account
Deploy a SAML 2.0 identity provider in every member account pointing back to on-prem Active Directory Federation Services (ADFS)
Configure AWS IAM Identity Center with the on-prem Active Directory as identity source (via AWS Managed Microsoft AD or AD Connector) and assign permission sets per account
Create IAM users in each account and run scheduled LDAP synchronisations from Active Directory to keep them up to date
questions.explanation: IAM Identity Center is the AWS-recommended pattern for multi-account, multi-app federated access from corporate identities: connect once to AD, map AD groups to permission sets, assign them to accounts, and users get a portal with short-lived credentials — minimal per-account work. Simple AD doesn't federate to your existing on-prem AD. Per-account SAML IdPs work but multiply configuration and trust 30+ times. LDAP-synced IAM users keep long-term credentials and lose all SSO benefits.

questions.question: A security engineer is designing attribute-based access control (ABAC) in AWS. The policy should allow EC2 actions only when the IAM principal's 'Department' tag matches the EC2 instance's 'Department' tag. Which condition key implements this?
options: Condition with StringEquals on ec2:ResourceTag/Department equal to the policy variable ${aws:PrincipalTag/Department}
Condition with StringEquals on aws:RequestTag/Department equal to ${ec2:ResourceTag/Department}, applied at request time
Condition with StringEquals on aws:PrincipalTag/Department equal to ec2:InstanceTag/Department, referencing the instance directly
Condition with StringEquals on iam:TagKey equal to the literal string 'Department' to gate the action by tag presence
questions.explanation: ABAC compares principal tags against resource tags using a policy variable: ec2:ResourceTag/Department compared to ${aws:PrincipalTag/Department} is the canonical form for 'principal and resource must share the Department tag'. aws:RequestTag is for tags supplied on the request (e.g., create-with-tag), not for matching an existing resource tag. ec2:InstanceTag isn't a real condition key. iam:TagKey only tests whether a key was supplied on a tagging API and doesn't compare values.

questions.question: A company runs a web application on EC2 instances behind an ALB. AWS Shield Advanced is enabled. During an active DDoS attack, the application is still degrading. What actions can the security engineer take to leverage Shield Advanced's capabilities?
options: Upgrade the EC2 instances to larger instance types so the application can absorb the additional attack traffic
Add CloudFront in front of the ALB during the attack, on the basis that Shield Advanced only protects CloudFront and not ALBs
Manually create WAF rate-based rules based on the attacking source IPs identified from CloudWatch metrics, and apply them to the ALB
Open a high-severity case with the AWS DDoS Response Team (DRT) via the support console so they can engage with custom WAF rules and live attack analysis
questions.explanation: Shield Advanced subscribers get 24/7 DRT access — opening a high-severity case engages the team to do live attack analysis, build custom WAF mitigations and adjust Shield policies during the attack. Scaling instance types isn't a DDoS mitigation strategy. Shield Advanced does protect ALB/NLB/EIP/CloudFront, so the 'CloudFront only' premise is wrong. Manually authoring rate-based rules works as a stopgap but doesn't leverage Shield Advanced's distinctive DRT capability.

questions.question: A company has multiple AWS accounts managed under AWS Organizations. The security team wants to implement AWS Control Tower guardrails to prevent any account from creating public S3 buckets. Which type of Control Tower guardrail should be applied?
options: A proactive guardrail using CloudFormation Hooks to block public S3 bucket configurations in IaC templates before they deploy
A preventive guardrail implemented as a Service Control Policy that denies the API actions that would make S3 buckets public
A detective guardrail that detects public S3 buckets after the fact and writes findings to the Security Hub dashboard
An elective guardrail that account administrators can opt into per account for additional public-S3 detection coverage
questions.explanation: Control Tower's preventive guardrails are implemented as SCPs and block the API actions in real time — exactly what 'prevent public S3 bucket creation' means. Proactive guardrails (CloudFormation Hooks) catch only the IaC path and not console/CLI/SDK actions. Detective guardrails report after the fact and don't prevent. 'Elective' isn't a Control Tower guardrail type associated with preventing public S3 buckets.

questions.question: A company stores sensitive PII in DynamoDB. The legal team requires that specific fields (SSN, DOB) be encrypted client-side BEFORE the data reaches AWS, and AWS staff should never see plaintext values. Which approach achieves this?
options: Enable DynamoDB encryption at rest with a customer-managed KMS key so AWS infrastructure cannot read the underlying storage in plaintext
Use DynamoDB server-side encryption (SSE-KMS) with a CMK so that data is decrypted only when the application requests an item
Have Amazon Macie continuously scan DynamoDB tables and automatically encrypt any sensitive fields it detects in place
Use the AWS Encryption SDK (or the DynamoDB Encryption Client) in the application to encrypt SSN/DOB attributes before PutItem, so DynamoDB only ever stores ciphertext
questions.explanation: Client-side encryption means the application encrypts the specific attributes locally (with KMS-protected data keys) before sending them to DynamoDB, so neither DynamoDB nor any AWS operator ever sees plaintext — exactly the requirement. DynamoDB encryption at rest (with or without a CMK) decrypts plaintext on AWS-controlled hosts when reading. Macie discovers sensitive data, it doesn't perform client-side encryption.

questions.question: A permission boundary is attached to an IAM role. The role's identity-based policy allows s3:* on all resources. The permission boundary only allows s3:GetObject and s3:PutObject. What is the effective permission for the role?
options: Only s3:GetObject and s3:PutObject — the effective permission is the intersection of the identity-based policy and the permission boundary
Only s3:GetObject — boundaries impose a minimum-permission set rather than a maximum, and s3:PutObject doesn't appear in both
Full s3:* — the identity-based policy grants full S3 access and takes precedence over the permission boundary
No permissions at all — boundaries deny everything unless an action is explicitly listed both in the boundary and in the identity policy
questions.explanation: Permission boundaries cap the maximum permissions an IAM entity can ever have; the effective set is the logical AND (intersection) of the identity-based policy and the boundary, so s3:* ∩ {GetObject, PutObject} = {GetObject, PutObject}. Boundaries cap maximums, not minimums. Identity policies don't override boundaries. There is no 'must be in both' rule beyond the intersection — which is exactly what option A states correctly.

questions.question: A security engineer discovers that an S3 bucket contains sensitive data and is configured with a bucket policy that allows public read access. The engineer also sees that a VPC endpoint policy for S3 restricts access to only specific accounts. How does traffic from an EC2 instance in the VPC to this S3 bucket behave?
options: The EC2 instance can read every object because the bucket policy already grants public access for all principals
The EC2 instance cannot access the bucket because the VPC endpoint policy always takes precedence over any bucket policy
Both policies are evaluated and access is allowed only if BOTH the VPC endpoint policy AND the bucket policy permit the request
The VPC endpoint policy only applies to cross-account access; same-account access through the endpoint uses just the bucket policy
questions.explanation: For requests that traverse a VPC endpoint, both the endpoint policy and the resource (bucket) policy are evaluated and access requires Allow from both — the endpoint policy is an additional filter on top of the bucket policy. Public bucket access doesn't override the endpoint policy. There is no general 'endpoint > bucket' precedence rule beyond joint evaluation. Endpoint policies apply uniformly, not just cross-account.

questions.question: A company wants to enforce that all new EC2 instances launched in AWS accounts must use only AMIs from an approved AMI catalog maintained by the central security team. What is the MOST scalable preventive control?
options: Deploy the AWS Config rule 'approved-amis-by-id' in every account with auto-remediation that terminates non-compliant instances after launch
Author identity-based IAM policies in each account that deny ec2:RunInstances when the AMI ID is not in the approved list
Use AWS Service Catalog with approved EC2 products and apply SCPs that deny direct ec2:RunInstances unless launched via Service Catalog
Apply an SCP across the organization denying ec2:RunInstances when ec2:ImageID is not in the approved AMI list, updating the SCP each time the catalog changes
questions.explanation: Service Catalog is the AWS-recommended self-service mechanism for vetted patterns: approved products encapsulate AMI choices and security configuration, and an SCP forcing all launches through Service Catalog scales as a preventive control without listing AMI IDs anywhere. Config-rule remediation is detective and reactive (instances launch then get terminated). Per-account IAM policies don't apply to all principals and must be maintained per account. An SCP that hard-codes the AMI list works but needs constant updating as AMIs rotate — Service Catalog avoids that maintenance.

questions.question: Security Hub is enabled with the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices (FSBP) standard. A company's security score is 62%. The security engineer wants to identify the most impactful controls to fix first. What approach increases the score most efficiently?
options: Sort failed Security Hub controls by severity (CRITICAL first, then HIGH) and within those prioritise the controls with the highest count of failed resources
Focus on INFORMATIONAL severity findings first because they are usually the most numerous in the report
Enable the CIS and PCI DSS standards in addition to FSBP first, then re-prioritise once you have a broader finding set
Fix whichever controls have the shortest estimated remediation time regardless of their severity weighting in the score
questions.explanation: The Security Hub security score is a severity-weighted ratio of passed-to-total controls; the biggest score gains come from fixing CRITICAL/HIGH controls that are failing on many resources, so sort by severity then by failed-resource count. INFORMATIONAL findings are weighted least. Enabling more standards first dilutes attention and doesn't help the existing 62%. 'Shortest remediation time' ignores the severity weighting that drives the score.

questions.question: A company has a Lambda function that needs to access a Secrets Manager secret. The function is deployed in multiple accounts. What is the MOST efficient way to share the secret across accounts while maintaining encryption?
options: Store the secret in SSM Parameter Store with a cross-account resource policy and have each Lambda fetch it from the central account
Create an IAM role in the secret's account that each remote Lambda execution role can assume, then call GetSecretValue once assumed
Export the secret value via a deployment pipeline and store a copy in each account's own Secrets Manager
Add a Secrets Manager resource policy to the secret allowing the other accounts' Lambda execution roles to call GetSecretValue, and grant kms:Decrypt on the CMK to those same roles
questions.explanation: Secrets Manager supports a resource-based policy on the secret; granting cross-account Lambda execution roles GetSecretValue plus kms:Decrypt on the encrypting CMK lets the remote Lambdas read directly without role assumption hops. SSM Parameter Store can do cross-account but lacks Secrets Manager rotation features. Role assumption works but adds latency and is more code than the direct resource-policy approach. Copying secrets per account multiplies the surface area and rotation problem.

questions.question: A company requires that all API calls to AWS are made only through approved network paths (corporate network or VPN). An SCP should deny any API call not originating from the approved IP ranges (203.0.113.0/24 and 198.51.100.0/24). Which SCP condition correctly implements this?
options: Deny '*' with NotIpAddress on aws:SourceIp = [the two approved ranges] plus a Null check on aws:ViaAWSService to skip AWS service calls
Allow '*' with IpAddress on aws:SourceIp restricted to [203.0.113.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24] so only those source addresses are ever permitted by the policy
Deny '*' with IpAddress on aws:SourceIp = [203.0.113.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24] so calls from inside the listed corporate ranges are blocked instead
Deny '*' with StringNotEquals on aws:SourceVpc set to a specific VPC ID to restrict the entire organisation to traffic from that single VPC
questions.explanation: The right pattern uses NotIpAddress (deny when source IP is NOT in the approved set) combined with a Null check on aws:ViaAWSService so AWS-internal service-to-service calls (CloudFormation→EC2, Lambda→S3) aren't blocked by the user-IP check. An Allow-only SCP is wrong because SCPs control deny semantics on top of identity Allows. IpAddress (option C) would deny the approved ranges — the opposite of intent. aws:SourceVpc restricts by VPC, not by corporate IP range.

questions.question: A company's security team wants to identify all IAM roles, S3 buckets, and Lambda functions that grant access to principals outside their AWS Organization. Which AWS service continuously monitors and reports this external access?
options: Amazon Macie scanning configuration data of IAM, S3 and Lambda for resource policies that grant external access
Amazon GuardDuty with IAM protection enabled, which detects external access to all resource types from policy evaluation
AWS IAM Access Analyzer with the zone of trust set to the entire AWS Organization, continuously analysing resource policies for external-grant findings
AWS Config with a custom rule that inspects resource policies for external principal ARNs on a periodic schedule
questions.explanation: IAM Access Analyzer is the purpose-built service: pick a zone of trust (account or organisation), and it continuously analyses resource-based policies on IAM roles, S3 buckets, KMS keys, SQS, Lambda, Secrets Manager and others and reports any grants to principals outside the zone. Macie focuses on data classification in S3. GuardDuty IAM protection detects credential abuse anomalies, not policy-grant external access. A custom Config rule could be built but isn't continuous and is custom code rather than a managed solution.

questions.question: A developer needs read access to an S3 bucket in Account B from an EC2 instance in Account A. The bucket policy in Account B already grants s3:GetObject to Account A's EC2 role ARN. However, the GetObject calls are still failing. What is the MOST likely missing configuration?
options: Versioning must be enabled on the bucket in Account B because cross-account reads require object versioning to expose object metadata
The EC2 instance's IAM role in Account A must have an identity-based policy allowing s3:GetObject on the specific bucket ARN in Account B
Account A must create a VPC endpoint for S3 to enable any cross-account bucket access from instances inside the VPC
Account B must accept a VPC peering connection from Account A's VPC before S3 cross-account requests will succeed
questions.explanation: Cross-account S3 access requires Allow from BOTH sides — the bucket policy in Account B AND an identity-based policy on the IAM role in Account A; granting only the bucket policy is the most common mistake. S3 has no dependency on versioning for cross-account reads. A VPC endpoint changes the network path but isn't required for cross-account access. VPC peering is irrelevant — S3 traffic doesn't traverse VPC peering.

questions.question: A company uses Amazon Cognito User Pools for their mobile application authentication. They want to ensure that after a user's account is compromised and their password is reset, any existing JWT tokens are immediately invalidated. What is the MOST direct approach?
options: Delete the user account from the User Pool and recreate it so all previously issued tokens are no longer recognised
Rotate the User Pool's JWT signing key as a global action so all currently outstanding tokens become unverifiable
Call the Cognito AdminUserGlobalSignOut API for the affected user, which invalidates all access, ID and refresh tokens across every device
Shorten the User Pool's JWT access token expiry to one hour so the previously issued compromised tokens expire quickly on their own
questions.explanation: AdminUserGlobalSignOut is Cognito's documented mechanism for immediate per-user token revocation: it invalidates every outstanding access, ID and refresh token for that user across all devices. Deleting and recreating the user loses profile/group state and is more destructive than needed. The User Pool signing key isn't a per-user revocation lever — rotating it would invalidate every user's tokens. Shortening expiry is reactive and doesn't immediately revoke already-issued tokens.

questions.question: A company's security audit finds that IAM users have more permissions than they actually use. The security team wants to right-size IAM permissions to implement least privilege. Which AWS tool identifies unused IAM permissions over the past 90 days?
options: GuardDuty IAM protection findings, which highlight overprivileged credentials and unused IAM users in the account
IAM Access Advisor (Last Accessed Information), which shows the last time each service was accessed by an IAM entity over the last 90 days
AWS Trusted Advisor security checks, which include an overprivileged-IAM-user check in the security category
AWS IAM Access Analyzer policy validation, which inspects policies syntactically for known security issues and findings
questions.explanation: IAM Access Advisor (also reachable via GetServiceLastAccessedDetails) records the last-accessed timestamp for each service per IAM entity over the past 90 days (and per-action for many services) — that's the dataset you use to remove permissions no one is exercising. GuardDuty detects threats and anomalies, not unused permissions. Trusted Advisor doesn't have a per-action unused-permission report. Access Analyzer policy validation flags policy syntax/security issues, not usage data.

questions.question: A company needs to enforce that all S3 buckets created in their accounts use SSE-KMS encryption and have public access blocked. New accounts joining the organization must automatically comply. Which combination achieves this with ZERO manual per-account configuration?
options: Deploy Lambda functions per account triggered by S3 bucket creation events to enforce the encryption and public-access settings after the fact across the organisation
Use an SCP denying s3:CreateBucket without SSE-KMS, plus organisation-level S3 Block Public Access, plus a Config conformance pack via StackSets with auto-deployment
Create a CloudFormation StackSet that deploys a baseline S3 bucket policy template to every existing account and re-applies the template whenever a new bucket is created
Use AWS Control Tower detective guardrails to flag S3 buckets without encryption or with public access enabled and rely on the SecOps team to remediate each finding manually
questions.explanation: The zero-touch enforcement combination is: an SCP that denies bucket creation without SSE-KMS headers, organisation-level S3 Block Public Access for all accounts (current and future), and a conformance pack deployed via StackSets with auto-deployment for new accounts. Per-account Lambda after the fact is reactive. A StackSet that 'deploys bucket policies on creation' isn't natively triggered by bucket events. Detective guardrails report after the fact and require manual remediation.

questions.question: A company's application uses API Gateway integrated with Lambda. The security team wants to log all API calls including the request and response bodies for security investigation purposes. What configuration is required?
options: Configure a Lambda authorizer in front of the API and log requests inside the authorizer function before authorisation runs
Enable CloudTrail data events for the API Gateway resource so request and response payloads are captured for every invocation
Enable API Gateway execution logging at INFO level on the stage and rely on it to capture full request and response bodies
Enable API Gateway access logging to a CloudWatch log group with a custom log format that includes $context.requestBody and $context.responseBody
questions.explanation: Access logging on the API stage with a custom log format including $context.requestBody and $context.responseBody is what captures the bodies; the log format is fully customisable per stage. A Lambda authorizer runs only on the request side and only for the bits the authorizer sees. CloudTrail captures API Gateway management API calls (creating/updating APIs), not invocation payloads. Execution logging records API Gateway's internal processing trace, not full request/response bodies.

questions.question: A company is implementing a data lake on S3. The data governance team requires that all data queries and who accessed which datasets be audited for HIPAA compliance. Which S3 logging mechanism provides the most detailed per-request audit trail including the requester's identity?
options: Amazon Macie running on the data lake buckets to classify sensitive data and surface access patterns by user activity
S3 server access logging delivered to a target bucket, capturing requester, bucket, key, action and status code for each request
CloudTrail S3 data events, recording every GetObject/PutObject/DeleteObject with the IAM principal ARN, account ID, source IP and object key
VPC Flow Logs on the subnets that host workloads, capturing network traffic to/from the S3 VPC endpoint for after-the-fact correlation
questions.explanation: CloudTrail S3 data events give the strongest audit trail for HIPAA: the IAM principal ARN, account, source IP, object key, action and timestamp for every object-level request, with log file integrity validation and centralised aggregation across accounts. Macie classifies data but isn't a per-request audit log. S3 server access logs can have delivery delay and don't always include the full IAM principal ARN. VPC Flow Logs see network 5-tuples, not the IAM identity or object key.

questions.question: A company deploys Lambda functions using infrastructure-as-code. Security policy mandates that Lambda execution roles follow least privilege and must be reviewed quarterly. The team wants to detect when a Lambda function's execution role has permissions broader than what the function actually used in the past 90 days. Which approach enables this analysis?
options: Use IAM Access Analyzer policy generation against the Lambda execution role to synthesise a minimal policy from the last 90 days of CloudTrail activity
Manually compare CloudTrail entries for the role against its current attached IAM policies and identify actions never observed
Enable GuardDuty Lambda protection, which flags Lambda execution roles whose permissions are broader than actual usage
Use the AWS Config managed rule 'lambda-function-public-access-prohibited' to check that the role's permissions stay within the function's usage
questions.explanation: IAM Access Analyzer policy generation analyses up to 90 days of CloudTrail activity for an IAM entity and emits a minimal policy of exactly the actions used; diffing that against the existing attached policy surfaces overprivilege. Manual CloudTrail-vs-policy comparison is what Access Analyzer automates and is feasible but the question asks for the AWS-native automated approach. GuardDuty Lambda protection detects runtime threats (suspicious calls), not policy-vs-usage drift. The named Config rule checks resource-level public exposure of Lambda, not role permission breadth.

questions.question: An organization receives a subpoena requiring them to preserve all AWS account activity logs and prevent any modification or deletion for 5 years. Which architecture satisfies this legal hold requirement?
options: Store CloudTrail logs in an S3 bucket with Object Lock in Compliance mode set to a 5-year retention period, with MFA Delete enabled as defence in depth
Enable CloudTrail and configure standard versioning on the target S3 bucket so previous versions are retained for the duration of the hold
Enable CloudTrail log file integrity validation so the logs are cryptographically tamper-evident and can be admitted as evidence
Archive CloudTrail logs to S3 Glacier Deep Archive and rely on the Glacier storage class being immutable after 90 days have elapsed
questions.explanation: S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode delivers true WORM: not even the root account can shorten the retention or delete the objects until the timer expires, exactly matching a legal hold. Standard versioning preserves old versions but any authorised user can delete them. Log file integrity validation detects tampering but doesn't prevent deletion. Glacier Deep Archive isn't intrinsically immutable — its 'minimum storage duration' is a billing concept, not a delete protection.

questions.question: A company's KMS key policy currently allows only specific IAM users to use the key. A new Lambda function in the same account needs to use the key for encryption. The Lambda has an execution role. What is the MINIMUM change required to the KMS key policy?
options: No change needed — every IAM identity in the same account can use any KMS key in the account by default
Add the AWS account root ARN ('arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT:root') to the key policy to enable account-wide IAM delegation
Create a KMS grant for the Lambda execution role using kms:CreateGrant rather than editing the key policy
Add the Lambda execution role ARN to the key policy with kms:GenerateDataKey and kms:Decrypt permissions for the specific role
questions.explanation: KMS key policies must explicitly authorise every principal — unlike S3, IAM policies don't grant key access unless the key policy itself includes the root ARN to enable IAM delegation. Since the existing key policy only lists specific users, adding the Lambda role with the required actions (GenerateDataKey + Decrypt) is the minimum, targeted change. Adding root ARN works but is broader than necessary — the question asks for the minimum change for this one Lambda. A grant works but the question scopes to a key policy change.

questions.question: A company wants to prevent developers from disabling GuardDuty, Security Hub, or Config in any account in their AWS Organization. What is the MOST effective way to enforce this?
options: Enable AWS Config managed rules that detect when these services are disabled and trigger an SNS notification to the security team for manual response
Apply SCPs at the organization root or OU level that deny guardduty:DeleteDetector, securityhub:DisableSecurityHub and config:StopConfigurationRecorder for all accounts
Attach IAM permission boundaries to every IAM user in member accounts that deny the disable-actions for those three services across the organisation
Configure EventBridge rules in each account to detect disable events and trigger Lambda functions that re-enable the services automatically
questions.explanation: Only an SCP at the organisation root or OU level is a true preventive control across every principal in every member account — including account-level admins and root users — so the disable APIs simply fail. Config-rule notifications and EventBridge-driven re-enabling are detective and reactive (a window of disabled state always exists). Permission boundaries only constrain individual IAM entities they are attached to and don't apply to root users; they're not an organisation-wide control.

questions.question: A security architect is designing a secrets management strategy for a containerized microservices application on Amazon ECS (Fargate). Secrets (database passwords, API keys) should not appear in container environment variables, task definitions, or application logs. Which approach follows AWS best practices?
options: Use Secrets Manager and reference the secret ARN in the ECS task definition's 'secrets' parameter so ECS injects the value as an environment variable at container start
Store the secrets in an encrypted S3 bucket and have the application container download the secrets file at startup before it begins serving traffic
Store secrets in AWS Secrets Manager and have the application call GetSecretValue via the SDK at runtime under the task's IAM role, keeping the value in memory only
Store the secrets as container environment variables encrypted with a Fargate-managed key so the values are only decrypted inside the container runtime
questions.explanation: Best practice on ECS Fargate is for the application to retrieve secrets at runtime via the Secrets Manager SDK using the task IAM role and keep them in memory only — that way secrets never appear in the task definition (which lands in CloudTrail/state) nor in container env vars (which 'docker inspect' or process listings can leak). The 'secrets' parameter in the task definition does inject the value as an env var, which violates the constraint. S3-based file download writes the secret to the container's filesystem. Container env vars 'encrypted with a Fargate-managed key' isn't a real mechanism — env vars in the task definition are visible.

questions.question: A security engineer needs to prove to a PCI DSS auditor that multi-factor authentication (MFA) is enforced for all AWS console access. The engineer has 15 accounts in an AWS Organization using IAM Identity Center with Active Directory as the identity source. Where is MFA enforced in this architecture?
options: Enable 'require MFA' in the IAM security settings of each individual AWS account so it applies to every IAM user across the organisation
Create an SCP at the organisation root that denies all actions when aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is false on the calling principal
MFA is enforced at the Active Directory layer (e.g., AD MFA, RADIUS or ADFS) and IAM Identity Center inherits that during the federated sign-in
Enable IAM Identity Center's built-in MFA policy so MFA is required at sign-in to the AWS access portal for every assigned user and account
questions.explanation: IAM Identity Center has a native MFA enforcement policy — required for all users, context-aware or disabled — and it applies centrally to the AWS access portal sign-in across every assigned account, which is the canonical way to enforce MFA in this architecture. Per-account IAM 'require MFA' settings don't cover Identity Center federated principals. An SCP based on aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent breaks because federated principals may set the context differently and SCPs only apply to API calls, not portal sign-in. AD-layer MFA can also work but the question is about IAM Identity Center as the architectural enforcement point.

questions.question: A bucket policy denies all requests where aws:SecureTransport is false. Which TWO additional controls would you add to BLOCK accidental public exposure of objects in this bucket?
options: Enable S3 Block Public Access at the bucket level to override any policy or ACL that would grant public read
Enable default S3 server-side encryption with SSE-S3 so newly uploaded objects are encrypted at rest by default
Enable S3 Object Ownership set to 'Bucket owner enforced' so ACLs are disabled and uploaders cannot grant public access on individual objects
Enable versioning with MFA Delete so deletion of object versions requires an MFA-authenticated root call
questions.explanation: Block Public Access overrides any bucket policy or ACL that would grant public access, and 'Bucket owner enforced' Object Ownership disables ACLs entirely so per-object ACL grants can no longer make individual objects public. SSE-S3 protects data at rest but doesn't gate access — public reads of encrypted objects are still served decrypted to authorised callers. MFA Delete protects against accidental version deletion, not against public reads.
